implementation_notes: std::atomic<T> with an explicit std::memory_order is the native form, and the language adds three things C does not have: the memory order is a compile-time-enforced type constraint (a failure order stronger than the success order is a diagnostic), atomic<T> is not copyable so the invariant 'always accessed atomically' is structural, and the default is seq_cst so a forgotten argument is safe rather than fast. std::atomic<T> is lock-free only for types where is_lock_free says so - std::atomic<double> typically calls a library function. In C++20, std::atomic_ref<T> brings the same guarantee to a field inside a larger object, and wait/notify_one/notify_all add blocking on top of the same state.
idiom_name: std::atomic<T> with std::memory_order; std::atomic_ref<T> for embedded fields
pitfalls: std::atomic<T> is not copyable, so storing atomics in a vector needs a wrapper or a std::atomic_ref; the ergonomics cost is real and often why people fall back to a mutex.
For types without a lock-free implementation (atomic<double>, atomic<struct>), the operation calls into libatomic and the code becomes blocking - check is_always_lock_free with a static_assert.
std::atomic<T> guarantees thread-safety for that object only: a plain field next to it is not covered, and the class must not be memcpy'd or moved while accessed.
A seq_cst store on x86 compiles to XCHG (a full barrier); defaulting to seq_cst for a counter in a hot loop can cost more than the cache miss it was meant to avoid.
